title: Bramblefoot's Moonlight Plan
markdown:
Way up in the Amberglow Mountains, where sunbeams painted the hills like honey and marmalade, lived Bramblefoot. He lived in a cozy cave, just right for him and his best friend. He was no ordinary ogre. Feet soft as moss. Heart as warm as toast. He liked to hum happy tunes, like a rumbling tummy. Big kind eyes twinkled with fun.

His best friend was Pip, a little mouse whose whiskers wiggled with every thought and whose tail wagged with joy. Pip was so small he could sit in Bramblefoot’s pocket, or even ride on Bramblefoot’s nose, whiskers tickling a chin.

One evening the moon peeked out, round and bright like a big white button. Bramblefoot hummed. “Pip, my little Pip.” Soft and happy, like a warm hug. “Tonight is special. I have a clever plan to make our walks even brighter.”

Pip’s whiskers went fast. “A plan? What sort of plan?” Tiny bell.

“A light-finding plan!” Cheeks puffed. “I’ve been watching the moonbeams. So sparkly. I think I can catch some moonlight in this jar.” A big empty jam jar with cheerful bees on it. “Then we can see the wobbly stones in the bluebell wood. No more stubbed toes. No more bumping sleepy bluebells.”

Pip giggled, little bells. “Magic! Can I help hold the jar?”

“Of course.” The jar strapped on. “We’ll go now, while the moon is high and the bluebells are sleepy. Just a little wander to test my plan.”

Soft feet padded, quiet as a whisper. Pip peeked from the pocket, nose twitching. Pine trees rustled like old friends sharing secrets. Fresh sweet air. The path glowed softly.

In the bluebell wood the flowers glowed with a sleepy light, and Bramblefoot saw something else: a little cottage, warm golden, cozier than moonlight. Outside, a kind lady tended herbs, wobbly pointy hat, a happy hum. Witch Hazeltoe. Eyes as kind as shiny pebbles. A smile that could warm a heart. She helped lost ladybugs find their way home.

“Good evening!” Rustling leaves. “What a lovely walk. And what a big sparkly jar.”

Bramblefoot shuffled mossy feet. “Good evening. I’m trying to catch moonlight in this jar to help us see the path.”

She looked in. “Moonlight-catching? A grand idea. But what do you think happens to something as quick and playful as moonlight?”

He thought hard. “It might dance away? Or get tangled up?”

“Just so!” Warm chuckle. “Moonlight loves to dance. It doesn’t like being kept in a jar. It splashes and plays everywhere. It would wiggle right out.” From her basket, a little sprig that smelled like warm cookies. “Glow-worm’s Delight. It grows where glow-worms dance. Hold this, and it makes a soft gentle glow. You’ll see the path without scaring the moonlight.”

The sprig gave a friendly light, like a tiny candle, and smelled of warm honey. Pip poked out. “Ooh, pretty!”

“Oh!” Bramblefoot’s face lit. “It helps me see the stones and roots. Even better than my plan.” He looked at the empty jar. “My plan wasn’t quite right. This is a wonderful discovery.”

Hazeltoe winked. “That’s the curious thing about plans. Sometimes you learn new things. And you might meet a helpful friend. Off you go. Enjoy your glow-worm-lit wander. Say hello to the moon for me.”

They kept walking. With Glow-worm’s Delight in hand, the wobbly stones were easy to see. Moonlight still twinkled on the leaves. Bluebells slept, unbumped. Pip snuggled in the pocket. Bramblefoot hummed his softest ogre tune. The jar on his back stayed empty on purpose, which is a kind of catching too.

Soon the cave welcomed them, a warm smile in the mountainside. Pip into the mossy bed. “That was a wonderful adventure.” Bramblefoot rumbled. He did not add a speech about friends being the best part. He set the sprig in a cup of water by the door, where it glowed just enough for a midnight toe.

Pip, already sleepy, twitched. “The bestest part,” he squeaked, and meant the pocket, or the glow, or the unstubbed toes, and did not have to choose.
